messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was sixty-five, a stocky man with tired eyes who had worked the checkout line at a downtown grocery for nearly twenty years. Five years ago, a tornado ripped through his neighborhood while he was alone in the back storeroom, counting inventory. The lights went, the metal shelves buckled, and the concrete walls groaned as though the whole building would collapse on him. He lay flat on his belly, hands over his head, praying—and for twenty minutes he was certain he would die. When the storm passed, he walked out into shattered glass and a sky that looked wrong, and something in him never really walked out again.

In the months that followed, Kwame’s sleep unraveled. He lay rigid in bed, listening for the low rumble of wind, convinced that if he let his guard down another storm would catch him unaware. His wife, Grace, would touch his shoulder and he’d flinch. The world, he came to believe, was a dangerous place—one that could turn violent without warning—and that conviction seeped into everything. He began scanning the ceiling of his bedroom for structural weaknesses; he checked weather alerts hourly. The belief that he had permanently changed for the worse made the memories of the tornado feel more immediate, as though they were happening right now rather than years ago. And each time a memory surged—the sound of shelving twisting, the smell of wet concrete—it only deepened his certainty that the world was no longer safe.

At work, Kwame started positioning himself so that he had a clear line of sight to the front doors, the side exit, and the emergency door near the dairy coolers. He scanned for exits as soon as he entered any room, his eyes tracing the fire escape route even while he rang up a customer’s groceries. The hypervigilance became automatic: he was watchful, on guard, never fully present. This constant state of alert kept his body keyed up, and when his heart raced for no obvious reason, the memory of the tornado would burst into his mind—the shudder of the floor, the pressure in his ears—so that he felt he was reliving it all over again. In turn, each replay reinforced his sense that the world was inherently hostile, that he had to be on guard every second.

He developed small routines to manage the fear. He always stayed close to an exit, even at home; he refused to sit in a restaurant booth unless he could see the door. When a memory threatened to take hold, he distracted himself—counting ceiling tiles, calculating the total of a grocery order, anything to push the image away. But the distraction itself left him feeling weak, as though he could no longer trust his own mind, which confirmed his belief that he had been permanently damaged. And the habit of staying near exits, of never fully relaxing, only made his hypervigilance worse: by never letting himself feel safe, he kept his guard up constantly.

His marriage suffered. Grace grew quiet when he insisted on checking the basement before bed, when he woke her by sitting up in the dark to scan the window. She stopped touching his shoulder. Kwame knew he was pushing her away, but he could not stop. The world was dangerous, and he had lost the part of himself that had ever felt otherwise. What finally brought him to a therapist’s office was a single moment: a customer dropped a case of canned beans, and Kwame dove behind the register, heart slamming, convinced the ceiling was falling. His manager found him crouching, panting, and asked if he needed to go home early. Kwame said yes, and he knew then that the loop—the memory driving the fear, the fear driving the vigilance, the vigilance driving more memory—had tightened around him for good. He came to the appointment hoping for something, though he could not name it; he was most afraid that nothing would change, that he would spend whatever years he had left scanning for an exit that never came.
